title: How To Handle Students Who Play Around In Time-Out n-time-out/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin lays out a sequence of guidelines for preventing and responding to students who goof around while in time-out. He argues the root cause is usually that expectations for time-out weren't clearly modeled, so the fix starts with reteaching exactly what compliant, ready-to-return behavior looks like. He advises removing the audience (addressing any peer who engages with the misbehaving student), pausing before responding to avoid rushing over emotionally, and simply observing from a distance to let the student self-correct. Only if misbehavior continues does the teacher escalate to a behavior letter home, with the entire process meant to feel calm, predictable, and detail-driven.
points: Most time-out misbehavior stems from unclear or under-modeled expectations, not defiance—so the first fix is reteaching the plan in detail.
Students should be taught they must sit quietly for at least fifteen minutes before requesting to rejoin the class.
If a peer engages with a student in time-out, the peer receives an immediate consequence to remove the 'audience' effect.
Rather than rushing over, teachers should pause and calmly observe from about ten feet away, letting quiet presence prompt self-correction.
Continued misbehavior after observation escalates to a behavior letter home and the remainder of the day in time-out.
quotes: So you send a student to time-out and almost immediately they start goofing around.
Nine times out of ten, students play around in time-out because you haven’t clearly defined what will happen if they don’t sit quietly.
Be sure your students understand that they must prove to you they’re ready to leave time-out—which includes sitting quietly and attentively for at least fifteen minutes
If another student communicates in any way with the student in time-out, then enforce a consequence immediately. This too must be modeled.
Your students need to know from beginning to end what will happen if they misbehave, which then must be as sure as the stars in the sky.
